Worked for 3m 55s

Yes—I’d choose this topic over the cascade-calibration question for G2i. It draws on much more of your actual work: structured ingestion, ArangoDB/Qdrant recall, QRA quality, provenance, and the recurring problem of keeping memory consistent. It also gives developers working on coding agents, search, or knowledge systems an entry point.

But I would not post it unchanged. Your strongest argument is “invest in what becomes reusable knowledge,” not “long context and RAG are the wrong architectures.” The latter goes further than the comparisons you’ve described establish.

The version I’d post

Hot take from running agents daily: before giving your agent more context, improve what it’s allowed to remember.

For my long-running agents, the useful shift has been from dumping material into the context window—or retrieving isolated chunks—to querying structured, source-linked knowledge.

My memory service uses ArangoDB for entities, relationships, and lexical search, paired with Qdrant for vectors. The agent queries it through a tool: lexical + semantic retrieval + graph traversal, with a path back to the original source when the evidence isn’t sufficient.

The work I keep coming back to is ingestion: extracting useful structure, resolving identities, preserving provenance, and deciding which generated Q&A pairs or inferred relationships deserve admission. I don’t want a model’s plausible interpretation quietly becoming a “fact” that every later agent retrieves.

This isn’t “RAG is dead”—it’s still retrieval-augmented. And the graph isn’t magic: bad extraction, stale knowledge, and graph/vector desynchronization are real problems in my setup. I still want agents reading the actual source, not treating memory as a replacement for it.

For people who’ve compared these on real workloads: where has ingestion-time structure actually earned its keep over strong hybrid retrieval or agentic repo search, and where has the simpler approach won?

I’m especially interested in the smallest amount of structure that made a measurable difference, including the cost of extraction, updates, and keeping it correct—not just answer quality on a static benchmark.

What needed correcting

“Both mainstream approaches treat the model as the searcher” is the wrong distinction. In ordinary RAG, a retrieval system performs the search; in your system, the model still chooses or formulates queries. The meaningful differences are what you index, how you retrieve it, and what evidence the result carries. Hybrid lexical/vector retrieval and contextualized chunks were already documented approaches in 2024—not just “embed raw chunks and hope.” 
Anthropic

“Teach the agent to query” is useful, but not the novel part in 2026. Anthropic’s September 2025 engineering guidance already described just-in-time context loading, tool-driven exploration, and coding agents using filesystem search rather than loading everything upfront. That is also a serious alternative to your graph: letting the agent inspect current source directly. Your interesting question is when the additional ingestion and memory machinery pays for itself. 
Anthropic

The ingestion emphasis does align with current research—but not as a rejection of raw context. The September 1, 2026 revision of Learning to Remember constructs reusable structured memory, explicitly maintains it through create/update/delete/reorganize operations, and answers using both memory and raw context. It supports investigating proactive memory maintenance; it does not establish that a graph database is universally necessary. 
arXiv

Replace “confidence too low” with “insufficient supporting evidence.” Otherwise, you bring the earlier calibration problem into this question: what makes that confidence trustworthy? A relevant August 30, 2026 preprint, PAGE-RAG, explicitly distinguishes graph connectivity from answer support: a relationship between retrieved candidates is a hypothesis about support, not proof of it. That distinction closely matches the provenance and answerability boundaries you’ve been working on. 
arXiv

Drop “prep is 80%” and “the query side almost takes care of itself.” The first reads like a measured allocation you haven’t supplied; the second conflicts with your own graph/vector consistency and evidence-gating work. Keep the personal observation—ingestion has demanded substantial effort—without implying retrieval is solved.

Finally, I would remove “multimodal from day one” from this particular post. It describes a relevant choice in your system, but prescribing it for everyone opens an unrelated architecture debate.

There are also current counterexamples worth explicitly inviting. A September 4, 2026 compact-memory preprint reports 83% of full-context quality at 32% of its token cost on one benchmark, while finding no statistically significant improvement over BM25-RAG on another. That is a quality–cost tradeoff, not “structured memory beats everything.” These are reported benchmark results, not validation of your deployment. 
arXiv

The question worth putting to the community is where structure earns its maintenance cost. That could tell you what to simplify or strengthen in your actual system, rather than merely collecting agreement that context dumping is bad.

Sources
what do you think about this edit from kimi: Final polish pass — here's the posting-ready version, with a few last tightening touches marked below:

---

**Hot take from running agents every day: before you give your agent more context, fix what it's allowed to remember.**

Here's where I've landed after a lot of trial and error. The winning move wasn't stuffing more material into the context window, and it wasn't feeding in whatever chunk a retrieval system happened to surface — a paragraph of text, a frame from a video, thirty seconds of audio with no transcript to check it against. It was teaching the agent to query structured, source-linked knowledge across all of it, and treating memory as something you curate, not something you dump.

My setup: ArangoDB holds entities, relationships, and lexical search; Qdrant handles vectors over text, images, audio, and video. The agent queries both through one tool, blending keyword matching, semantic search, and graph traversal. When the evidence isn't enough, it can always trace back to the original source — the actual clip, the actual document.

That combination has proven genuinely useful in practice, and mostly for one reason: the agent never has to take memory's word for anything. With non-text media especially, there's often no clean text to verify a guess against — so the path back to the source is what makes memory trustworthy rather than just searchable.

The real work — and I keep coming back to this — is ingestion. Getting good structure out of raw material, resolving who's who, keeping provenance intact, and being picky about what gets in. Generated Q&A pairs, inferred relationships: those get admitted carefully, because a model's plausible guess has no business becoming a "fact" that every future agent retrieves and builds on. And it gets harder the moment you leave plain text — "what does this clip actually show?" is an extraction step where confidence and correctness easily drift apart.

Honest caveats, because I've hit all of these: this isn't "RAG is dead" — it's still retrieval, just with better plumbing. The graph is not magic. Bad extraction happens. Knowledge goes stale. Graph and vector stores fall out of sync. And agents should still read the actual source — memory is a shortcut to it, not a replacement.

**The question I'm genuinely curious about:** if you've compared these on real workloads, where has ingestion-time structure actually paid off versus strong hybrid retrieval or agentic repo search — and where did the simpler thing win?

I'm especially after the smallest amount of structure that made a measurable difference — extraction cost, update cost, correctness upkeep included, not just answer quality on a static benchmark. And if you've gone multimodal: what was the minimum structure that made images, audio, or video actually retrievable and *trustworthy*, rather than just searchable?

---

What the final pass changed:

- "Here's what I've landed on after" → "Here's where I've landed after" — slightly more natural spoken rhythm.
- "makes the memory trustworthy" → "makes memory trustworthy" — drops a syllable, reads cleaner.
- The "trustworthy rather than just searchable" line now deliberately echoes the closing question — the post argues in a circle that closes on the ask, which makes the ending feel earned instead of tacked on.

If you want a tighter cut for X (roughly half the length, same beats) or a copy saved as a file for your notes, just say so.

It’s a good prose edit, but I’d tighten it before posting. The opening is strong, and “memory is something you curate, not something you dump” captures your experience well. But Kimi has turned a focused discussion question into a small essay—and introduced a couple of claims that deserve more caution.

The worthwhile final pass is not “drops a syllable.” It is shorten the setup, distinguish traceability from correctness, and keep the implementation claims bounded.

What I would change

“Auditable,” not “trustworthy.” This is the most important correction:

“The path back to the source is what makes memory trustworthy rather than just searchable.”

A source link lets you check an interpretation; it does not establish that the interpretation is correct. The source could be ambiguous, the extraction wrong, or the relationship unsupported. Your actual principle is stronger when stated precisely:

A path back to the source makes memory auditable. It doesn’t make the extracted claim true.

Similarly, “the agent never has to take memory’s word for anything” describes an available verification path—not evidence that the agent actually follows it. “I treat memory as a route to evidence, not as authority” avoids that overclaim.

Keep multimodal, but don’t expand the implementation claim casually. “Qdrant handles vectors over text, images, audio, and video” implies working ingestion and retrieval across all four modalities. I wouldn’t strengthen your claim that far based on the implementation evidence you’ve shared. Retrieving a transcript, retrieving a frame, and retrieving source-anchored audio/video evidence are distinct capabilities. “Qdrant handles vectors” is sufficient for the architecture paragraph; the multimodal discussion can then focus on the requirement that matters: returning the relevant original evidence.

The multimodal comparison needs a broader baseline. Once the post covers documents, images, audio, and video, “agentic repo search” is no longer the right comparator for the whole workload. Use “strong hybrid retrieval or direct source search.” Repo search remains one instance of that simpler approach.

Keep one central question. The draft asks both “when does structure pay off?” and “what makes multimodal retrieval trustworthy?” They’re related, but either could dominate the discussion. Make the first the question and multimodal workloads an especially interesting case.

The version I’d post

Hot take from running agents every day: before you give your agent more context, fix what it’s allowed to remember.

What’s helped me most hasn’t been a bigger context window or more retrieved chunks. It’s been giving agents a tool to query curated, source-linked knowledge—and treating memory as something you maintain, not something you dump.

My setup uses ArangoDB for entities, relationships, and lexical search, with Qdrant for vectors. Recall combines lexical matching, semantic search, and graph traversal. But I treat memory as a route to evidence, not as authority.

The hard work is ingestion: extracting useful structure, resolving identities, preserving provenance, and deciding what deserves admission. Generated Q&A pairs and inferred relationships shouldn’t silently become “facts” that every future agent builds on.

That boundary matters especially with multimodal material. A searchable description of a clip isn’t necessarily a faithful account of it. I want retrieval to point back to the relevant page, frame, or time span—not just a model’s summary. Source links make memory auditable, not automatically correct.

This isn’t “RAG is dead.” It’s still retrieval, and the graph isn’t magic. I’ve hit bad extraction, stale knowledge, and graph/vector desynchronization. More structure also means more things to keep correct.

For people who’ve compared these on real workloads: where has ingestion-time structure earned its maintenance cost over strong hybrid retrieval or direct source search—and where has the simpler approach won?

I’m especially interested in the smallest amount of structure that made a measurable difference, counting extraction, updates, and correctness maintenance—not just answer quality on a static benchmark. Multimodal examples would be particularly useful.

This keeps what makes your experience interesting without making you defend the much broader claim that structured memory is inherently trustworthy or generally superior. It also invites answers that could genuinely change your implementation—including evidence that some of its structure is not worth maintaining.

reasoning_text:
Worked for 6m 3s
1. Is the approach sound and genuinely effective?

Yes as a confinement architecture; not yet as an unconditional promise of “employer compliance stays green while all other-client information stays private.” AppArmor can meaningfully constrain a root process. Root does not automatically override its mandatory access controls, and removing capabilities reduces the privileges available to the confined process. These are substantive controls, not cosmetic restrictions. 
AppArmor
+1

I would retain the architecture. The owner-approved plan, executable identity binding, positive-and-negative probe, and parked-OFF recovery are good design choices. My concerns are about what the boundary includes, how long its evidence remains valid, and whether “green” still represents a meaningful check.

This is an assessment of the described design—not an independent qualification of your running host or a claim that any particular bypass has been demonstrated.

The two goals must be established independently

Your objective has two distinct requirements:

Requirement	What must actually be established
Confidentiality	The agent and any components acting for it cannot obtain protected client information through the permitted filesystem, process, IPC, network, or cached-data surfaces.
Valid compliance	Every required check obtains sufficiently complete, fresh, truthful inputs and the employer accepts the resulting assessment.

A service being active establishes neither. A green dashboard does not establish confidentiality, and a successful denied-read probe does not establish valid compliance.

The combination is achievable where the required checks and the protected data are separable. If a required check genuinely needs information inside a protected client workspace, an allowlist cannot simultaneously disclose and withhold that information. The choices become an explicitly agreed narrower check, a supported minimal-information interface, or a different work environment—not another sandbox flag.

OS enforcement is the right layer

Using an OS boundary rather than relying entirely on collection settings is justified. Current 1Password documentation explicitly distinguishes restrictions on viewing features from restrictions on collection: disabling a feature does not necessarily stop its data collection. Its table blocklist also does not retroactively affect existing queries, including official checks. Those controls can complement your boundary, but they are not equivalent to it. 
1Password

I would therefore keep default-deny rather than replace it with “allow everything except a few sensitive directories.” However, the default-deny policy needs to cover interfaces, not just file trees. An agent that cannot open a document directly may still receive its contents from an allowed service.

“Never spoof telemetry” is necessary, but not sufficient

There is an important distinction between:

The confinement tool never invents a result.

and:

Every denied data source is represented accurately as unavailable throughout osquery, the check evaluator, and the employer’s dashboard.

The first is under your tool’s control. The second requires end-to-end testing. Osquery aggregates heterogeneous sources; the vendor itself warns that result values and missing-data assumptions require care. 
Kolide

For example, a hypothetical check that treats “no offending rows returned” as success could become misleading when the scanner cannot inspect the relevant objects. That is a false-green risk, even though your confinement tool has not fabricated a byte.

I would make preservation of check meaning—not preservation of dashboard color—the compatibility criterion.

2. The material efficacy gaps
A. Loopback permission is substantially broader than browser identification

The browser’s need is narrow: connect to the agent’s local identification server and complete the genuine protocol. The vendor documents that local server and its role in identification and behavior changes. That does not establish a need for the agent to initiate connections to every other localhost service. 
1Password

Systemd’s IPAddressAllow/IPAddressDeny rules filter IP addresses in both directions; they do not distinguish browser-initiated handshakes from agent-initiated connections or restrict access to one application port. Allow entries take precedence over deny entries, and unmatched addresses are allowed. Consequently:

With only private/VPN ranges denied, public destinations remain allowed.

With IPAddressDeny=any and only loopback allowed, direct public phone-home traffic is blocked unless separately permitted.

The effective behavior also depends on the surrounding slice configuration and working kernel enforcement. 
manpages.ubuntu.com

The privacy consequence: a blanket loopback allowance can expose unrelated local APIs, development servers, databases, or forwarding services. Whether any actually reveals protected data depends on its authentication and permissions; their existence is a review target, not a demonstrated bypass.

I would replace “localhost is trusted” with a narrowly enforced connection policy: preserve the genuine browser-to-agent endpoint and necessary replies, while denying unrelated agent-initiated local connections. Use a mechanism that can express that distinction; an address-only exception cannot.

Test IPv4 and IPv6, unrelated local listeners, and network/VPN transitions with synthetic services. Also prove that the filter is operating: systemd documents that these IP settings can have no effect when the required support is unavailable. 
Ubuntu Manpages

B. Filesystem confinement does not automatically close IPC and process visibility

The named directory denials are valuable, but I would explicitly review process information, system and session buses, administrative sockets, abstract Unix sockets, and any permitted helper service.

PrivateIPC isolates System V IPC and POSIX message queues; it is not a general prohibition on Unix sockets or D-Bus. ProtectSystem=strict primarily establishes read-only mounts, not confidentiality. Those settings cannot substitute for explicit read and communication restrictions. 
Ubuntu Manpages

The key question is:

Can an allowed peer obtain information for the agent that the agent cannot obtain directly?

Unix sockets can convey data, file descriptors, and peer credentials. Their permission boundary deserves its own treatment rather than being inferred from denied directory names. 
man7.org

Running as UID 0 remains relevant even with zero capabilities. Removing CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE removes a permission override; it does not change ownership or revoke access already granted by ordinary permissions. Nor does it make every external service stop recognizing the caller as root. 
man7.org
+1

Two specific cautions:

Do not interpret an AppArmor owner rule as “this process only.” It is an ownership condition, not a process-identity condition. Review broad process-path grants accordingly. 
Ubuntu Manpages

Do not add ProtectProc=invisible and assume the problem is solved. The systemd documentation warns that root is unaffected by that option. For a root service, explicit process-access restrictions and their live tests remain important. 
Ubuntu Manpages

Where compatible, a dedicated non-root identity would reduce these ambient relationships. Where root is genuinely required, compensate with narrower interfaces—not assumptions about what dropping capabilities accomplished.

C. Hash-pinned executables do not mean behavior-pinned collection

Your executable hashes answer “which code did the owner approve?” They do not answer “which questions will that code be asked tomorrow?”

Device Trust supports remotely supplied live queries and recurring queries. Its log pipeline supports additional query packs and configurable collection. The same unchanged executable can therefore exercise different approved interfaces without any binary drift. 
1Password
+1

This creates two separate risks.

Availability: a newly scheduled query reaches a denied resource and fails, stalls, or exposes an agent error.

Privacy: a new query extracts more information from a resource that was already allowed. No sandbox escape is necessary; the grant was broader than the intended purpose.

A first-hour test is useful but not sufficient. Osquery schedules can extend to a week, discovery conditions can activate packs later, and scheduled timing depends on daemon runtime rather than simply elapsed wall-clock time. Some scheduled work does not execute at startup. 
osquery

I would maintain a required-check inventory containing each check’s data sources, freshness requirement, expected behavior on missing inputs, and permitted disclosures. Where remote queries cannot be frozen or fully inventoried, bound the confidentiality claim by the resources accessible to any query—not just the queries observed during testing.

D. Self-update is an unresolved lifecycle requirement, not an incidental nuisance

The immutable executable paths are valuable. But the vendor’s agent explicitly includes automatic updates for its components, using TUF to authenticate update targets. A vendor-authenticated update establishes provenance; it does not establish compatibility with your owner-approved access boundary. 
1Password

There are three distinct cases:

Update behavior	Architectural consequence
The confined agent cannot replace or execute the update	The boundary may hold, but the agent needs a supported maintenance path rather than becoming indefinitely stale.
New code executes while retaining the same confinement	The privacy boundary may hold, but required behavior and check meaning need requalification.
An updater or installer runs outside the boundary	That component has separate authority and may invalidate the confinement assumptions.

I would not solve update failures by granting execution throughout writable state or opening a generic privileged maintenance interface. That would weaken precisely the boundary the immutable-code rule is intended to establish.

Instead, make updating an explicit owner-controlled transaction: obtain authenticated artifacts, review the changed execution and resource requirements, install without an unconfined interval, rebuild the binding, and repeat qualification.

The approved code set should include relevant helpers, extensions, and executable mappings—not merely the initial launcher. AppArmor distinguishes executable transitions and executable mappings, so inspecting only the main executable is not a complete execution-boundary review. 
Ubuntu Manpages

Most importantly, state the trust limit: a profile around one service does not constrain an independently privileged host installer. If the threat model includes malicious code executed with unrestricted host-administration authority, this service-level mechanism alone is insufficient.

E. Allowed state can contain protected information already

“The agent’s own state” is an operational category, not a guarantee about the sensitivity of its contents. Osquery stores scheduled-query results locally for subsequent comparison. Information collected before confinement may therefore remain in storage the new policy still permits. 
osquery

A newly effective deny rule does not erase prior local collection or retract remote copies. Assess preexisting agent state and support/diagnostic artifacts separately, using an approved process rather than blindly deleting enrollment or evidentiary material.

More generally, the policy follows accessible resources, not the business ownership of their contents. A copy of a client secret placed in an allowed location remains accessible under that grant. That is not a kernel bypass; it is a limitation of the information boundary.

I would distinguish three claims in the evidence:

Direct content access is denied. Metadata disclosure is bounded. Previously collected data has been assessed.

Do not combine them into a single “protected directory” checkbox.

F. Legitimate posture metadata can still violate the intended privacy boundary

A check can legitimately consume information that is sensitive in context. Account names, installed software, process details, identifiers, and network configuration can reveal affiliations or activity without exposing a source file.

“OS posture” therefore needs a disclosure budget: which fields, from which sources, for which check, with which residual inference risk? AppArmor file permissions are not generally a field-level redaction mechanism. 
Ubuntu Manpages

The machine-ID presets especially need restrained claims. Systemd explicitly treats the machine ID as confidential and recommends application-specific derivation rather than directly exposing the raw identifier. But removing one read does not establish anonymity or remove an already enrolled device’s identity. 
Ubuntu Manpages

I would rename compliance-safe to something like compatibility-baseline and define its exact disclosures. “Share what keeps the check green” is a dangerous optimization target because its endpoint can be continual permission expansion.

minimal-identity should mean a specific reduction in permitted identity inputs, not “the employer cannot correlate this device.” locked-down should describe its actual resource restrictions, not imply complete cross-client isolation.

G. Post-start fail-closed recovery is not the same as pre-execution prevention

Parking OFF after a failed check is the right recovery direction. But stopping a process cannot undo a read or transmission that occurred before the failure was detected.

Require effective controls before the first target instruction, not merely a later readback. Systemd’s AppArmorProfile requires a loaded profile, but the setting has no effect when AppArmor itself is disabled; error-suppressing configuration and privileged command exceptions also matter. 
Ubuntu Manpages

I would require the same invariant on boot, automatic restart, update restart, and recovery—not only on your tool’s initial apply. Every relevant helper must enter the boundary before operating. Periodic verification can bound the detection delay for drift; it cannot establish that no exposure occurred between checks.

Also separate expected access denials from loss of enforcement. A blocked optional read can mean the privacy policy is functioning. A missing profile or ineffective network filter means the boundary is not established. Automatically parking on every routine denial can turn legitimate restrictions into an outage loop.

3. Biggest risks, and what I would harden first

For ordinary vendor evolution, I would prioritize new query requirements, update transitions, and pressure to broaden access. For a compromised agent or adversarial collection request, I would prioritize excessive permitted resources, reachable privileged peers, collection outside the selected unit, and defects in the underlying kernel.

The kernel issue is not hypothetical in the abstract. Canonical’s 2026 CrackArmor advisory covers AppArmor kernel vulnerabilities and recommends both kernel fixes and userspace mitigations. Its separate Copy Fail advisory is another reason not to reduce platform qualification to “AppArmor loads successfully.” These advisories do not establish that your host is vulnerable; they establish that current running-kernel qualification matters. 
Ubuntu
+1

I would harden in this order:

Priority	Change	Acceptance gate I would require
1. Establish the complete execution boundary	Cover startup, helpers, restarts, updates, and independently launched collection components. Check the running kernel and enforcement prerequisites.	In a disposable qualification environment, missing mandatory controls prevent target execution; no target component operates outside the approved boundary.
2. Narrow loopback and IPC	Preserve the genuine browser handshake without granting unrelated local-service access. Review every permitted peer as a potential data source.	Browser identification succeeds; attempts against synthetic unrelated local services and unauthorized IPC peers fail under the actual service identity and controls.
3. Validate required-check meaning	Inventory required checks and distinguish complete results, unavailable inputs, stale data, and actual failures.	Controlled compliant and noncompliant fixtures produce the expected results; denied required inputs are never accepted as evidence of compliance.
4. Make updates a qualified transaction	Separate writable runtime state from approved executable content and make maintenance explicit.	A real update and restart preserve confinement and required functionality, or leave a clearly reported parked-OFF state without an unrestricted interval.
5. Minimize permitted information	Review state, process information, identifiers, diagnostics, and configuration by content—not just pathname.	Synthetic sensitive values outside the approved disclosure set do not appear in collected results or locally retained diagnostic artifacts.
6. Extend lifecycle evidence	Exercise scheduled work, reboot, suspend/resume, network changes, and agent maintenance. Protect the verifier and its evidence from the target.	Retained results identify the tested versions, policy, workloads, transitions, observation gaps, and actual check freshness.

These are proposed acceptance gates, not claims that the present implementation already meets them.

What I would not prioritize first

I would not begin by accumulating more isolated syscall denials. They can reduce attack surface, but they do not fix an overly broad permitted data source or a reachable service that discloses information. AppArmor’s own security guidance distinguishes resource-level mediation from brittle per-syscall filtering. 
AppArmor

Likewise, MemoryDenyWriteExecute and NoNewPrivileges do not make approved code trustworthy or restrict it to the owner’s intended business purpose. The latter specifically limits privilege gain through execution; it is not an application-behavior verifier. 
Ubuntu Manpages
+1

Shared-host timing and resource side channels also remain a residual category, but I would address direct authorized disclosures and local-service access first. Claiming noninterference between client workloads would require a much broader assurance argument than this design currently supplies.

The stronger architectural direction

For high-consequence cross-client confidentiality, my preferred long-term direction is a separate work environment that actually contains the employer’s workload, with no shared client directories, credentials, or broadly exposed integration channels. Device Trust must assess that real work environment—not a decoy environment used to obtain a green result for another machine.
